extracted.intended_audience: journalism professionals, nonprofit newsroom leaders, and readers interested in news-industry standards
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize the membership criteria and application process the Institute for Nonprofit News (INN) uses to admit nonprofit newsrooms, focusing on editorial independence, funding transparency, operational independence, and reporting quality. Also covers how applications are reviewed and approved.

rubrics_metrics.name: INN membership standards (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: INN membership standards focus on editorial independence and transparency and include prohibitions on "dark money" to fund journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: INN wants membership to be “a sign of quality, credible journalism” in an information ecosystem that includes bad actors (e.g., "pink slime" sites). To become a member, nonprofit news organizations must meet the membership standards and be approved by INN’s board of directors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants must have full editorial independence; lack of full editorial independence is cited as a common reason for denial (for example, if the newsroom is part of an advocacy-oriented nonprofit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: INN rejects organizations that do not have full editorial independence. The CEO emphasizes members produce independent, fact-based reporting distinct from advocacy-driven content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding transparency / prohibition on anonymous funding ('dark money')
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants should be transparent about funders; receiving too much anonymous funding ("dark money") is a reason for denial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: INN emphasizes you should "know exactly who their funders are." Prohibitions on dark money are part of membership standards to help distinguish members from misleading sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations must be operationally independent from a larger organization; being "not operationally independent from a larger organization" is listed as a reason for denial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational ties that impede independent newsroom functioning can disqualify an applicant; INN staff assess organisational structure during review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality of reporting must be high; "the quality of the reporting is not high enough" is cited as a reason for denial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: INN describes members as producing "fact-based, data-driven original reporting" and distinguishes such work from press releases, funder-prescribed content, or "pink slime" journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from funder-prescribed content
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsrooms must not produce content dictated by funders; producing press-release-style or funder-prescribed content is contrasted with the type of original reporting INN expects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEO Karen Rundlet framed INN members as different from "press releases, or funder-prescribed content," indicating editorial control over content is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application review and approval process (procedural requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each application receives hours of individual review from INN staff, who make recommendations; the INN board of directors has the final say on admission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: INN staff will work with newsrooms that have been rejected to help them try to meet the organization's standards on subsequent applications (second or third application). Board approval is required for membership even after staff recommendation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Membership as a signal of credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: INN frames membership as a public signal that a newsroom produces credible, independent journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Membership is intended to help the public distinguish INN members from low-quality or misleading sites; this is part of INN's mission to elevate independent journalism.
